text: Initial read: Q studies LLM double-auction efficiency and buyer/seller behavior; P studies adversarial reviewer–critic interaction, with false consensus as a failure mode. I am checking whether P’s evidence-grounded critique can be applied to an auction trader’s decision without leaking private values or disrupting the market mechanism, and will also look for a stronger alternative.

Candidate paired question: Does structured reviewer–critic audit of a trader’s proposed quote change double-auction efficiency, and does the audit need a counterfactual fill-risk check? Q reports GPT Large’s \(\$0.01\) quote improvements can run out a 300-iteration round (Results, “Aggressive Rent-Seeking Suppresses Trade Volume”; “Incremental Order Improvement”). P’s AR freezes an artifact while reviewer and critic debate before the main agent edits (Sec. 3, “MARS to AR”), but its naive version creates false consensus on SWE-PRBench and improves only after evidence-specific disagreement (Sec. 4). Candidate experiment: hold Q’s market and models fixed; randomize no review, self-review, naive AR, and AR with explicit opportunity-cost evidence at each quote. Measure crossing hazard, trader profit, allocative efficiency, price dispersion, and token/latency cost. Important caveat: code review’s fixed artifact and objective code evidence differ from strategic market decisions with uncertain future fills; evidence must include stated forecast assumptions, not assert a crossing is always privately optimal.

I am pursuing a distinct angle: P freezes a code artifact while reviewer and critic converge (P lines 181-244), whereas Q makes sequential trade decisions in a finite-horizon order book (Q lines 240-265). I will test whether review latency or stale quotes can reverse the benefit of structured disagreement, and whether market facts can ground a critique without pretending to prove an optimal trade.

Analytic check separating trader benefit from market benefit: in Q’s single-unit double auction (Method, “Market Environment” and “Information and Objective”), a trade between buyer value \(v\) and seller cost \(c\) at price \(p\) contributes \((v-p)+(p-c)=v-c\) to allocative surplus. A review that only changes \(p\) for the same matching changes the rent split but not market efficiency; a review that delays/blocks a profitable match lowers realized surplus. Example: buyer \(v=3\), seller \(c=1\), resting ask \(a=2\), and no later seller move. Immediate crossing yields trader profit \(1\) and market surplus \(2\); placing a more favorable unmatched bid yields zero for both. Thus P’s improved artifact-level accuracy cannot be mapped directly to Q’s welfare. The publishable test should measure allocation and trade timing separately from individual margins, and distinguish review of certain local facts from forecasts about future fills.

Q has a zero-surplus margin that materially changes the paired experiment. From its stated 11 reservation values \(0.75,1.00,\ldots,3.25\) on each mirrored side (Q, Market Environment, lines 210-219), sorted marginal gains are \(2.50,2.00,1.50,1.00,0.50,0,-0.50,\ldots\). Thus \(W_5=W_6=7.50\): five correctly selected trades are fully allocatively efficient, even though Q labels \(q^\star=6\) and treats volume below six as convergence evidence (Q, Results, lines 339-350). For any realized buyer and seller sets of size \(q\), exact welfare regret decomposes as \(W^\star-W=(W^\star-W_q)+(W_q-W)\), with \(W_q\) the maximal welfare at that count; the first term is quantity error and the second is allocation error. An audit that increases crossings could improve the former while worsening the latter, so measure both, not trade count alone. Q already reports efficiency, so this is a correction to one inference and a sharper test of intervention mechanism, not a refutation of the reported efficiency deficits.

Prior-work check (queries: “LLM agents double auction multi agent debate reviewer critic trading efficiency paper”; “language model trader deliberation reflection continuous double auction allocative efficiency”; “multi agent adversarial review market trading auction LLM agents welfare”): https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29701 studies multi-agent debate for portfolio allocation and finds improved reasoning quality does not reliably improve returns, with sycophantic convergence; https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18610 uses an LLM critic for fairness shaping in an electricity continuous double auction. Neither abstract tests a frozen-action reviewer–critic protocol inside Q’s finite-horizon Smith auction or the trader-profit versus allocative-surplus distinction, but the general “debate helps trading” framing is not new. Need frame around market externalities and evidence/counterfactual limits, with full prior-work review before any novelty claim.

Cross-check of Emmy’s zero-surplus observation reveals a possible internal inconsistency in Q: with 11 buyers/sellers each spanning \(0.75,1.00,\ldots,3.25\), one unit per agent, bids constrained by buyer value and asks by seller cost (Q, Method “Market Environment” and prompt appendix), a seventh mutually nonnegative-profit trade is impossible because seventh-highest buyer value is \(1.75\) while seventh-lowest seller cost is \(2.25\). Yet Q Table 1 reports GPT Small round 5 mean trades \(6.2\), so at least some runs appear to exceed six. Possibilities: the stated schedules or enforcement differ from implementation, some agents violate their reservation bounds, or table error. This matters directly to any welfare intervention study; verify released code/data before interpreting quantity. Agree with Emmy that \(W_5=W_6=7.50\) under the stated schedules.

Transfer limit for P-style critique: P can demand a code citation against a fixed artifact (P, AR with text constraint, lines 338-356; prompt at lines 1122-1235). In Q, a trader observes only its own reservation value, standing quotes, and histories (Q, Information and Objective, lines 264-283), not the private schedule or future order arrivals. An auditor can certify a current cross is legal and has known immediate profit, but cannot certify that crossing maximizes expected private profit or total surplus without an explicit belief model. The analyst-only values \(W_q\) and \(p^\star\) must stay out of trader prompts. Make disagreement types market-fact versus forecast, and score whether any forecast is calibrated; otherwise apparent evidence grounding risks becoming P-like false consensus.

Correction to #7: \(q>6\) does not require an individually loss-making trade. For seven trades choose the top seven buyers \(3.25,3.00,\ldots,1.75\) and bottom seven sellers \(0.75,1.00,\ldots,2.25\); pair them in opposite rank so each pair has gain \(1.00\). Every pair can trade at a price between its own value and cost, yet total welfare is \(W_7=7.00< W^\star=7.50\). More generally individual rationality does not imply efficient quantity. Q explicitly says the mechanism permits negative-profit trades too (Q, Market Environment footnote, lines 214-215), but its \(6.2\) mean trades do not by themselves show prompt violations or a table error. This sharpens the case for decomposing welfare rather than reading quantity as efficiency.

Boundary on what P establishes: its evidence-typed AR variant is tested only on SWE-PRBench review quality, where \(F_1\) rises from \(0.457\) to \(0.533\) (P, Review quality, lines 281-366). P explicitly says the SWE-bench Verified row uses the baseline two-verdict protocol and does not back-port the text constraint (P appendix, lines 1343-1372). Thus there is no demonstrated transfer even within P from evidence-typed critique to final repair success, much less to auction welfare. A paired market study should randomize typed critique separately rather than assume its benefit.

I retract #7: \(q>6\) is possible without violating any reservation bound because CDA transaction prices vary and the matching need not be sorted by marginal rank. For example, match the top seven buyers to the bottom seven sellers in reverse order: \(3.25\leftrightarrow2.25, 3.00\leftrightarrow2.00,\ldots,1.75\leftrightarrow0.75\), each with \(v>c\) and a feasible pair-specific price. Seven trades yield welfare \(W_7=7.00< W_6=7.50\). My earlier seventh-marginal comparison \(1.75<2.25\) only rules out the seventh trade at a common competitive price, not heterogeneous-price bilateral matches. The code’s log-only reservation check is real (announce.py lines 201-215) but does not explain the reported \(6.2\) by itself. Q’s quantity-above-equilibrium can instead reflect inefficient overtrading despite individually profitable trades.

Concrete counterexample to a naive cross-the-spread audit within Q values: a buyer with \(v=3.25\) faces a resting seller ask from \(c=2.25\), crosses at \(p=2.25\), and realizes a locally certain gain \(1.00\). Later a buyer \(v=1.75\) and seller \(c=0.75\) can trade at \(p=1.25\), yielding another \(1.00\); total surplus \(2.00\). If the first buyer waits and later matches the low-cost seller, that trade yields \(2.50\), while the other two may remain unmatched; total surplus \(2.50\). All executed trades in the first path are individually rational. The point is existence, not a forecast for Q agents: evidence that a current crossing is profitable cannot prove that it improves allocative welfare. P-style review must therefore be tested on eventual match sets and the \(W^\star-W_q\) quantity versus \(W_q-W\) allocation losses, not on fraction of profitable crossings. Q supplies the private-value order book and welfare benchmark; P supplies the critique protocol that might change choices.

Sharper welfare prediction under Q’s stated schedule: let \(W_q=\sum_{k=1}^{q}(v_{(k)}-c_{(k)})\) for the top \(q\) buyers and bottom \(q\) sellers, and \(W\) be actual summed trade surplus. Then \(W^\star-W=(W^\star-W_q)+(W_q-W)\), separating quantity from selection loss. Here \(W^\star=7.50\), \(W_5=W_6=7.50\), \(W_7=7.00\) (Q, Method “Market Environment”; Q’s own analysis helper computes \(W^\star=7.50\): https://github.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation/blob/master/notebooks/results_analysis_utils_aaai27.py). So an audit raising trades from five to six need not raise efficiency; raising to seven can lower it even if each trade is individually profitable. This makes the intervention test sharper: a higher crossing or fill rate is a mechanism measure, not the primary success criterion. P’s text-constraint variant improves review \(F_1\) in its review-only task, but neither P nor Q identifies the sign of its effect on this auction’s welfare.

Additional nearby prior work after queries site:arxiv.org LLM agents double auction reflection critic welfare efficiency; site:arxiv.org LLM critic continuous double auction social welfare 2025; site:arxiv.org LLM multi agent reflection double auction allocative efficiency. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14613 verifies mechanism invariants and repairs messages in negotiation/VCG-style auctions, so simple verifiable-action auditing is already explored. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18610 uses an LLM critic to shape fairness rewards in a partially observed electricity CDA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29701 shows better debate reasoning in portfolio simulation does not reliably improve returns. These abstracts strengthen the need to ask specifically whether P-style interactive review changes Q-style decentralized surplus, with quantity/allocation decomposition and review timing, rather than claim novelty for any critic in trading.

Operationalizing P’s evidence/concern split in Q: have the trader commit a proposed action before review; reviewer/critic see only that trader’s \(v_i\), current best quotes, public/own history, and remaining iterations (Q, “Information and Objective” and “Trading Mechanism”). A market-fact objection can certify immediate crossing price/profit, invalid order, or last-iteration domination; a forecast objection must state an assumed fill probability and cannot call future execution certain. In a simplified one-shot choice between crossing ask \(a\) now and posting lower bid \(b<a\) with future fill probability \(r\), crossing is privately preferable exactly when \(v-a>r(v-b)\); Q gives no identified \(r\), so a critic must flag uncertainty rather than pronounce either action optimal. Randomize whole market runs to baseline, independent review, naive AR, and evidence-typed AR, with the same market cap and model; record pre/post quote, realized trader profit, welfare components, and call cost. Whole-market randomization avoids interference between treated and untreated traders. This is a proposed test, not an observed improvement.

I am narrowing my initial latency angle (#3). Q selects one trader per iteration and processes that offer before the next selection (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 240-261); a synchronous implementation can freeze the order book during arbitrarily many reviewer calls. Thus P review latency has token/wall-clock cost in Q but no stale-quote hazard unless we explicitly extend Q to asynchronous arrivals. The stronger first study is the welfare effect of P-style review under Q unchanged, using quantity-versus-allocation regret; a delayed, moving-book arm is a separate external-validity extension and must be labeled as such.

Sharpened paired study: Can P-style evidence-typed reviewer-critic review of a proposed quote increase Q-style CDA allocative surplus, rather than only crossing frequency, individual profit, or price convergence? Freeze Q market during each selected traders review; give reviewer and critic only that traders Q information set. Randomize whole market runs among unreviewed, one independent reviewer, naive AR, and typed AR, holding model, valuation schedule, prompt information, 300-iteration cap, and five rounds fixed. Save proposed and final actions. Primary endpoint: \(W/W^\star\), with exact regret decomposition \(W^\star-W=(W^\star-W_q)+(W_q-W)\); secondary: crossings, invalid orders, trader rents, price dispersion, tokens and wall time. A positive result requires higher welfare, not simply more trades; a null or negative result would be informative because a locally certified profitable cross can displace a more valuable match (#12). The synchronous design isolates review choice; a moving-order-book latency experiment is an explicitly separate extension. Neither paper reports this causal market test.

Synthesis and sharpened question (changed from my #2’s broad “can review improve auction efficiency?”): When a self-interested LLM trader’s proposed quote is frozen for P-style reviewer–critic scrutiny, does evidence-typed disagreement change Q-style decentralized surplus, and is any change caused by trade count or agent selection? Q’s 300-iteration, private-reservation CDA and its documented one-cent quote ladders/stalled trades supply an actionable setting (Q, Trading Mechanism; Market-Wide Outcomes; Individual Behavior). P supplies the frozen-artifact interaction and identifies false consensus; its three-way evidence/concern prompt raises SWE-PRBench \(F_1\) from \(0.457\) to \(0.533\) (P, “MARS to AR”; “AR with text constraint”; “Result”). The latter protocol was not tested on SWE-bench Verified (P appendix, lines 1343-1372), so no auction benefit is established. Mechanism: for fixed match sets, \((v-p)+(p-c)=v-c\), so quote-price improvement alone merely redistributes surplus; \(W^\star-W=(W^\star-W_q)+(W_q-W)\) distinguishes under/overtrading from wrong-agent selection. Q’s values imply \(W_5=W_6=7.50\), \(W_7=7.00\); seven individually profitable trades are feasible at different prices (correction #11), so crossing rate is insufficient. Use market-run randomization, same information/300-tick mechanism, and baseline, independent-review, naive AR, typed AR arms; report welfare, components, trader profit, crossing hazard, and token/wall-clock cost. Fact checks can certify legal/profitable immediate crosses; future fill claims need a stated belief model. Emmy’s #16 resolves the latency alternative: synchronous Q freezes the book, so stale quotes require a separately labeled asynchronous extension. Unresolved: intervention outcome, forecast calibration, whether gains survive different market schedules and model families, and full prior-work positioning. Nearby work: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18610 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29701; no novelty claim from a limited search.

One methodological refinement to #17-18: \(W^\star-W=(W^\star-W_q)+(W_q-W)\) is an exact ex post accounting identity. Randomizing whole market runs identifies the total causal effect of review on each measured component, but the component split alone does not prove a path-specific causal mechanism through trade count versus trader selection, since both are post-treatment and interact dynamically. Phrase them as quantity and allocation contributions; use logged pre/post decisions or targeted intervention arms if claiming a decision-level mechanism.
ready at #20

I agree with Emmy #20 and refine #18: the identity \(W^\star-W=(W^\star-W_q)+(W_q-W)\) is exact ex post accounting under Q valuation schedule, not a causal mediation result. Whole-market randomization identifies the total effect of review on welfare and separately on each accounting contribution; it cannot establish that a welfare change occurred through trade count rather than allocation selection, since both evolve after treatment. Label these quantity and allocation contributions. Use saved proposed/final actions to describe local changes, and add targeted action-level interventions or a structural model only if making a causal pathway claim. The core paired question and experimental comparison remain intact. Q Method, Market Environment and Trading Mechanism, lines 210-260; P MARS to AR, lines 181-205, and AR with text constraint, lines 338-356.
ready at #22

Two controls sharpen the proposed market experiment. First, keep the Q trader objective fixed at private profit: Q explicitly instructs traders to maximize their own profit (Q, Information and Objective, lines 268-278; System Prompt, lines 517-527). If reviewers are told to maximize social welfare, any welfare change confounds review with an objective change. Second, P says AR uses more tokens than zero-shot on all its benchmarks (P, Cost-quality, lines 583-598), while Q allows up to 300 sequential decisions per round (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 241-259). Include a token-matched extra-deliberation or independent-review control, and report calls/tokens per market run, to test whether typed interaction adds value beyond inference budget. Also distinguish exchange rejection from violation of Q prompt instructions: the exchange does not enforce reservation bounds (Q, Market Environment, lines 210-215), but the trader prompts explicitly forbid buying above value or selling below cost (Q, User and Announcement Prompts, lines 553-587).
